transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you here today?

Well, doctor, my daughter brought me, but... I keep telling them, I keep trying to explain it to my family but they just won't listen to me. It's about my friend. She passed away recently, and... and I'm the reason she died. I just am. I know I am, and nobody will believe me. 

She called me, you see, and I had just gotten off a long shift at the register—I've been a cashier for years and years—and my feet were just aching so badly, so I saw the phone ringing and I just didn't pick it up. I told myself I was too tired. I didn't call her back. And then she was gone. But it's even worse than just the phone call, because... well, I used to have these ugly, awful thoughts sometimes. Just wicked things in my head that I shouldn't have been thinking about her, petty things, mean things. God knows what's in your heart, doctor. He sees the ugly thoughts, even the ones you never say out loud. 

And because of what I did, because of the wickedness in me... I know the Lord is punishing everybody at my church because of me. It's entirely my fault. The whole congregation is suffering. The church has been having all these troubles lately, and I just sit there in the pew on Sunday mornings knowing it's my sin bringing God's wrath down on all those good people. I brought this ruin on them. I killed my friend with my selfishness, and now God is striking down the whole church just to punish me, and I just don't know how to make it stop.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear?

No, doctor, no... it's not like that. I don't hear people whispering or anything like that, no voices in the empty rooms or anything. It's just my own heavy conscience, you see. It's the weight of what I've done. 

Sometimes I'll be sitting in my living room—the one with the floral wallpaper I put up back in '98, my husband helped me with it before he passed—and it gets so quiet in there you could hear a pin drop. Just the ticking of the old clock in the hall. And in that silence, I don't hear anyone speaking to me, but I just... I just know the truth. The silence is almost worse, really, because it just gives me more time to think about my friend, and that phone ringing. I remember the sound of the phone ringing, of course, that shrill ring from the kitchen wall phone, but that was real. That really happened. I just didn't answer it. I let it ring and ring because my feet hurt. 

So no, no voices from nowhere, just the absolute certainty of God's judgment on me. I don't need a voice to tell me I'm wicked when the proof is right there in front of me every Sunday at church. I just look at all those poor people suffering because of my selfish heart, and I know.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things that happened in the past, even when others told you it wasn't your fault?

Well, yes, doctor, that's... that's exactly it. That's what I was trying to explain before. My family, my daughter—bless her heart, she tries, she really does, she works so hard at the bank and still finds time to check on me—she keeps telling me I'm being silly. She says, "Mom, you couldn't have known," or "Mom, it was just her time." But they don't understand the weight of it. They don't know what it's like to carry this around all day, from the minute I wake up and put my slippers on until I lie awake at night staring at the ceiling fan. 

I keep telling them, I keep saying it over and over, but it's like talking to a brick wall. I am the reason she died. It wasn't just her time, it was my selfishness. If I had just answered that phone... I was so tired from standing at the register, you know how the linoleum floors just ruin your knees after a while, but that's no excuse. I let it ring. And it's not just the phone call, it's the thoughts I had. The ugly, spiteful little thoughts that creep into your mind when you're feeling uncharitable. I had those thoughts about her. And God sees all of that. He sees the blackness in my heart. 

And the worst part, the absolute worst part that I just can't bear, is that it's not just me paying the price. If it was just me, well, I'd deserve it. But I know, as sure as I'm sitting in this chair, that the Lord is punishing everybody at my church because of what I did. The roof leaking in the sanctuary, Pastor Miller's wife getting so sick last month, the youth group van breaking down on the highway... it's all connected. It's a plague on them, and I brought it to their doorstep. I sit there on Sundays in the third pew on the left, the same spot I've sat in since 1982, and I look at all those good, faithful people, and I just know it's my fault they're suffering. I'm a wicked woman, doctor, and no matter how many times my daughter tells me it's not my fault, I know the truth. I just know it.
Over the last two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, yes, doctor... yes, I have. It's just a terrible heaviness, you see. It sits right here on my chest, right from the moment I open my eyes in the morning. And it's every single day. I'll wake up—usually around 5:30, because that's when my husband used to get up for his shift at the plant, and my body just never forgot the routine even after all these years—and before I even swing my legs out of bed, the darkness just rushes in. 

It's like a thick fog in my house. I'll shuffle into the kitchen to make my oatmeal, the same plain oatmeal I've eaten every morning since my stomach started acting up in my sixties, and I just stand there at the counter crying. Just weeping into my bowl, because I can't find a single reason to feel anything but sorrow. I don't even turn the television on anymore. I used to love my morning programs, you know, the ones with the recipes and the nice hosts who always look so put together, but now the noise just feels wrong. It feels inappropriate to have anything cheerful in the house when I'm so full of this... this misery. 

It lasts all day, doctor. I'll sit in my armchair by the window, the one where the sunlight usually comes in so nicely around 2 o'clock, but I don't even notice the sun anymore. I just sit there and feel so low, so utterly defeated by what I've done, by the wickedness I'm carrying. My daughter will call on her lunch break, and I try, I really do try to sound normal for her, but she can hear it in my voice. She says I sound hollow. And she's right. I feel hollowed out, just empty and sad and tired... so very tired all the time. It doesn't lift in the evening, either. It just stays with me, dragging me down, making it hard to even breathe sometimes, until I finally go back to bed and stare at the ceiling fan again. So yes, every day... it's just this constant, heavy sorrow.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy, like your morning TV shows or other activities?

Well, yes, doctor, I... I suppose I have. I mentioned the television programs, but it's really everything. It's just everything. I used to be such a busy woman, you know. I was always doing something. 

I was in the church choir for forty-two years. Forty-two years! I stood right in the second row, next to Betty Higgins. We used to sing "How Great Thou Art" and I'd feel this wonderful lift in my spirit, just so happy to be there singing praises. And the knitting circle on Tuesday afternoons... oh, we used to have such a lovely time. I made a beautiful yellow afghan for my grandson when he was born, with the little cable knit pattern that took me three weeks to get right. We'd sit and drink Earl Grey tea and talk about the neighborhood. And Thursday nights was bingo at the community center. I wasn't a big gambler, mind you, just a few cards, but I loved the social part of it, seeing everyone, having a laugh when the caller would make a joke. 

And on nice days, especially in the spring when the dogwoods were blooming, I used to love walking through Patterson Park. I'd put on my good walking shoes—the white ones with the arch support because of my knees—and I'd walk all the way around the duck pond. I used to bring a little bag of oats for the ducks, because bread isn't good for them, you know. 

But now... now I don't do any of it. None of it. I just sit in my chair by the window. The knitting needles are still in the basket next to the sofa, right where I left them months ago. Betty called twice to see if I was coming back to choir, but I couldn't even bring myself to call her back. I just... none of it feels worth getting dressed for anymore. Putting on clothes, brushing my hair, putting on a bit of lipstick... it all just feels so pointless when my soul is so heavy. Why would I go sing hymns or play bingo when I'm carrying this terrible burden? It wouldn't be right. And honestly, I just don't have the energy or the desire to even try. It's all just gone.

Doctor: Do you believe that your guilt or sins are being punished in a way that goes beyond what other people might experience, such as divine punishment or causing events that others wouldn’t be responsible for?

Well, yes... yes, I do. It’s exactly that, doctor. I know it sounds... well, I don't know how it sounds to you, but I know what I hear and I know what it means. I told you before about sitting in that third pew on the left, right? The one with the little scratch on the wood near the hymnal rack that my husband accidentally made with his watch band back in 1989. Well, I sit there now, and I just... I listen to Pastor Miller. He’s a good man, Pastor Miller, he really is, he's been with us for fifteen years since Pastor Thomas retired to Florida. But lately... lately when he stands up there at the pulpit, right under the big stained glass window of the Good Shepherd, and he bows his head for the pastoral prayer... I know he’s not just praying for the congregation in general. 

He says these things, these specific lines about hidden sins and the Lord's judgment falling upon the house of God... and I know. I just know he’s warning me. He's speaking right to me. He knows, and God knows, that I've been marked. Like Cain, you know? Marked for what I did and for the ugliness inside me. 

And it’s not just the pastor, doctor. It’s the choir, too. Remember I told you I sang with them for forty-two years? I know all the arrangements, I know all the soprano parts by heart. But now, when they stand up there in their burgundy robes—the ones we spent three whole years doing bake sales to afford—and they sing certain lines... it’s different. Last Sunday they sang that old hymn about a mighty fortress, and when they got to the part about the prince of darkness, Betty Higgins—she's the one I used to stand next to—she looked right at my section of the pews. I could feel it in my bones. They're singing those lines to warn me. 

They're telling me that God has marked me, and that all the suffering in the church, the leaking roof, Pastor Miller's wife being so ill... it's all because I brought this on us. I brought this terrible, wicked curse right into the sanctuary. They know it, and God knows it, and they're using the service to tell me that the whole church is paying the price for my black heart. I just sit there and clutch my purse, my knuckles go completely white, because how can I even look them in the eye when the very prayers and hymns are pointing the finger at me? I should just stay home, I tell myself I shouldn't even walk through those heavy oak doors anymore, but if I stay home, maybe God will punish them even worse for my absence. I just don't know what to do, doctor, I really don't. It's just so much to bear...
Have you had episodes of feeling this low before, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

Well, doctor... I mean, I've had sad days in my life, certainly. When my husband passed, bless his soul, I grieved, of course I did. But it was a normal grief, you know? It wasn't this... this terrible, punishing darkness. No, this feeling, exactly like this... it's the first time. And it's been going on for just about two months now. 

It started right after... well, ever since my close friend died. Her name was Martha. We had been friends for over fifty years, doctor. We met way back when we were both working the cash registers at the old A&P grocery store downtown, back when you actually had to punch the keys down hard, not like the laser scanners they have today. We did everything together. Every evening at 7 o'clock, right after Jeopardy finished, the phone would ring and it would be Martha, and we'd talk for at least an hour about everything and nothing. 

But then... she passed away, just two months ago. It was so sudden. The funeral was on a Tuesday, a very rainy Tuesday, and I remember coming home to my empty house and just feeling... different. Something shifted. The very next morning, I woke up at that 5:30 time I told you about, and the heavy feeling was just sitting right there on my chest, like a stone. And it hasn't lifted once. Not for a single minute in two whole months. Every day since we buried her, it's just been this endless, suffocating misery. I've never experienced anything like this in my entire seventy-four years on this earth, doctor, I really haven't. It's just been two months of pure, unbroken sorrow.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or unusually irritable, where it was different from your usual self?

Well, heavens no, doctor. No, I’ve never experienced anything like that. I’ve always been a very... well, a very steady sort of person. You have to be, you know, when you work the registers like I did. Thirty-two years I spent at that A&P, and you can't be flying off the handle or getting overly excited when you're dealing with the public and trying to count back exact change. I was always the reliable one. 

Now, my sister-in-law, Doris—my late husband's younger sister—she was the type who would get exactly like what you're saying. Oh, my goodness, she would have these spells where she’d be up at two in the morning rearranging all her living room furniture, dragging the heavy oak coffee table across the rug, or she'd suddenly decide to bake six dozen snickerdoodles for no reason at all. And irritable! If you even looked at her sideways during one of those moods, she’d snap your head right off. I remember back in the summer of '94, at the family picnic, she threw a whole plate of potato salad right in the trash just because someone said it needed a pinch more paprika. 

But me? No, no. I've never had anything like that happen to me. I never felt unusually high or bursting with energy out of nowhere. I liked my routine, doctor. I liked things predictable. I'd wake up at a normal hour, have my half grapefruit and my toast with a little bit of orange marmalade—the Dundee kind in the glass jar, not those awful plastic squeeze bottles they have now—and just go about my day. I was always just... even-keeled. Never bouncing off the walls or acting out of character. 

The only time I ever got irritable was if the arthritis in my knees was acting up right before a big thunderstorm, but anyone would be cranky with their joints swelling up like balloons. Aside from that, no. I've always just been my regular, quiet self. At least, I was, until this terrible heavy darkness settled on me...
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one—lasting at least two weeks—where you felt down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, no, doctor... I really haven't. Like I was saying about being an even-keeled sort of person, that went for my moods, too. I mean, sure, I've had times where I felt a little blue, like anyone else. When they closed down the old A&P and we all had to find new jobs, that was a sad time. I remember sitting at my kitchen table with my cup of tea—Earl Grey, always Earl Grey in the afternoons—just looking out the window at the neighbor's rhododendron bush and feeling a bit lost. But that only lasted a few days, maybe a week at most, until I got hired at the pharmacy down the street. 

But a whole two weeks? Two whole weeks of feeling hopeless every single day, all day long? No, never. Not until Martha passed. Before this, even if I was sad, I could still enjoy my evening programs, or I'd still want to go to my Tuesday morning quilting circle at the church. I made this beautiful double wedding ring quilt back in 2012, took me six months, all hand-stitched... but anyway, I always bounced back. I never had this... this relentless weight that just sits on you from morning till night, day after day, week after week. This is entirely new, doctor. Completely new and just... just awful.
Have you ever had any other periods in your life, even shorter ones, where you felt down or hopeless almost every day, even if it didn’t last as long as this current time?

Well, no, doctor... I mean, I really don't think so. I know I keep saying that, but it's the truth. Like I mentioned, there were little spells of sadness, like when the store closed, or when my husband passed away. But even then, even when I was missing him terribly, it wasn't this... this heavy, black cloud that just wouldn't lift. 

I remember when he died—it was back in '98, a heart attack, very sudden—I was devastated, of course. I cried every day for a while. But even in the middle of all that grief, I would still get up, make my bed, and go water my African violets. I had a whole row of them on the windowsill above the kitchen sink, beautiful deep purples and soft pinks. I was very particular about them, you know, you have to water them from the bottom or the leaves get all spotted and rot. And I still cared about them, even when I was mourning. I still cared if they bloomed. 

But this feeling I have now... it's completely different. It's not just being sad for a few days or even a week. It's like... like everything inside me has just stopped working. So, no, even for shorter periods, I've never felt this kind of absolute hopelessness before. Never. It's always just been normal sadness that comes and goes, like the weather. You put on a raincoat, you wait for the sun to come back out. But the sun just isn't coming out anymore, doctor. It really isn't.
Before this current period, has there ever been a time in your life when you felt so low that you had trouble functioning normally for a week or more?

Well, no, doctor... I really haven't. Like I was saying, I've always been the sort of person who just keeps going. Even when things were hard, I kept functioning. I had to, you know? There was always something that needed doing. The laundry doesn't wash itself, and the floors don't sweep themselves. 

I remember back in the winter of 2003, we had that terrible ice storm. Oh, it was just dreadful. The power was out for three whole days, and it was so cold you could see your breath right in the living room. I had to bundle up in three sweaters and a heavy wool coat just to sit on the sofa. And my joints were aching terribly from the cold, just terribly. But did I stop functioning? No, I did not. I got out the camping stove we kept in the garage from when my husband was alive—he loved to go fishing up at the lake, though I never cared for the mosquitoes myself—and I heated up cans of Campbell's chicken noodle soup. I even walked two doors down to check on Mrs. Higgins, because she was older than me and lived alone, and I wanted to make sure she wasn't freezing to death in her armchair. 

So, you see, I've always been able to function. I've always been able to do what needed to be done, whether I was sad or cold or tired. I never had a time where I was so low I couldn't get out of bed or manage my daily chores for a week. I'd still go to the grocery store, I'd still balance my checkbook—every penny accounted for, right down to the last cent—and I'd still make sure my house was neat as a pin. 

But now... oh, doctor, now it's just so different. I look at the dust gathering on the end tables, and I just don't care. I know it's there, I know I should get the Pledge and a rag, but my arms feel like they're made of lead, and my mind just keeps telling me there's no point. There's no point to any of it. So, no, I've never had trouble functioning like this before. This is... this is something else entirely.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period—before Martha passed—when you felt so down or hopeless that it interfered with your ability to live your normal life, even for just a couple of weeks?

Well... no, doctor. I know we've been going round and round about this, and you're trying to be thorough, which I do appreciate. Dr. Aris, my old general practitioner before he retired in 2015—lovely man, always wore those little bowties, usually with polka dots or little sailboats—he used to say you have to turn over every stone to find the real problem. But truly, turning over all the stones in my past won't find anything like this. 

Before Martha passed... well, life just went on. Even when it was difficult, it didn't stop me from living my normal life. I was always the one organizing the neighborhood potlucks, making sure everyone brought something different so we didn't end up with three potato salads. I make a wonderful ambrosia salad, by the way. My mother taught me how to make it when I was just a girl, with the little mini marshmallows and the mandarin oranges. You have to drain the oranges very well, or the whole thing gets soggy, and nobody wants a soggy ambrosia salad. 

But my point is, I was busy. I was active. I was at the grocery store four days a week, not just because I worked there, but because I liked seeing people. I liked chatting with Mrs. Gable at the checkout about her grandson's little league games. I liked feeling like I was part of the world. Even if I had a bad day, or felt a little down, it never stopped me from putting on a clean blouse, doing my hair—I used to get a roller set every Friday morning at 9:00 AM sharp at Betty's Curl and Swirl—and getting on with my day. 

I never, ever had a time where I couldn't live my life for a couple of weeks. Never. I wouldn't have allowed it, frankly. I would have thought it was just laziness or feeling sorry for myself. But now I know... now I know it's not that at all. Because I want to get up. I want to care about the ambrosia salad and my hair and Mrs. Gable's grandson, but I just... I can't. The life I used to live feels like it belonged to someone else entirely. So, no, nothing like this ever interfered before. This is the very first time the world has just... stopped.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period when you felt so down or hopeless that you had to stop doing some of your usual activities, even for just a short time?

Well, doctor, I know you’re just doing your job, asking it every which way to see if I remember something different, but I really, truly haven’t. I feel like a bit of a broken record, but I’ve never had to stop my usual activities because I was feeling down. Never in my life. I mean, I’ve had my heart broken, like I said, but I always kept my routine. 

I think about when my sweet dog, Buster, had to be put to sleep. Oh, this was years ago, back in... goodness, it must have been 1992. He was a Golden Retriever mix, the most beautiful golden coat, though he shed like you wouldn't believe. I had to run the Hoover over the living room rug every single day, sometimes twice if it was spring shedding season. But anyway, when his hips went bad and the vet—Dr. Evans, over on 4th Street—said it was time, I was just sick over it. Sick with grief. I came home with his empty red collar and I just sat at the kitchen table and cried until my eyes were nearly swollen shut. 

But you know what I did the very next morning? I got up at 5:30 AM, just like always. I didn't have Buster to walk, which broke my heart all over again, but I still made my percolator coffee—none of this instant nonsense, real ground coffee—and I still put on my name tag and went to my shift at the register. I even worked a double that Thursday because Shirley called out sick with a stomach bug. And on Sunday, I still made my pot roast. You have to sear the chuck roast first, you see, get a good brown crust on it in the skillet before you put it in the slow cooker with the pearl onions and the celery, otherwise the meat just tastes boiled and gray. 

So, no, I was terribly sad about Buster, but I didn't stop doing a single one of my usual activities. I kept the house clean, I went to work, I cooked my meals. I just pushed through it. That’s what a person does. But this thing I have now... it’s not something you can just push through. I couldn't make a pot roast right now if my life depended on it. The very thought of standing at the stove, of chopping a carrot... it just exhausts me down to my bones. So, no, doctor. I've never had to stop my life like this before. Never.
Have you ever experienced a time when you felt unusually excited, overly confident, or needed less sleep than usual for several days or more?

Oh, heavens no. No, I've never been that sort of person. Unusually excited or overly confident? That just isn't me, doctor. I've always been very level-headed, very down-to-earth. My mother used to say I was born middle-aged because I never had that wild, flighty phase most girls go through. Even back in high school, while the other girls were swooning over singers or staying up all night at slumber parties, I was just... well, sensible. 

And as for sleep... goodness, I have always, always needed my rest. You simply can't work on your feet for forty years at a cash register if you don't get your proper sleep. Your back gives out, your arches ache... no, I would go to bed at 10:00 PM on the dot, every single night. I had one of those digital alarm clocks with the red numbers—the kind that are so bright they almost keep you awake if you face them toward the bed, so I always had to turn mine slightly toward the little oak nightstand. And I would wake up at 6:00 AM. Eight solid hours. 

Even when something truly wonderful happened, like when my husband surprised me with a trip to Branson, Missouri for our 25th anniversary—which was just lovely, by the way, we saw some wonderful shows, though the seats in the theater were terribly stiff on the lower back—I still went to bed at my usual time. I didn't stay up all night buzzing with excitement or feeling like I could conquer the world. I just don't have that kind of... wild energy, I suppose. I've always been steady as a rock. Never too high up in the clouds. I just kept my feet on the ground and got my eight hours.
Has anything like this ever happened to you before—where you felt so low and unable to function—that lasted for weeks or months?

Doctor, I feel like we are sort of dancing to the exact same tune here, aren't we? I know you have to be absolutely sure, and I don't fault you for it. It’s a bit like when I used to train the new girls at the registers—I always told them, "You have to check the bottom of the grocery cart twice, every single time, because people will leave a heavy twenty-four pack of soda or a giant bag of dog food down there and just walk right out the door without paying." You have to check twice to be thorough. I understand that. 

But I promise you, checking the bottom of my cart again isn't going to turn up anything new. No. Never for weeks, never for months. 

I mean, of course I’ve had periods of mourning that lasted a long time. When my mother passed away... oh, goodness, that was back in 1998. It was a terrible, bitter winter that year, ice on all the roads, and the city actually ran out of salt for the snowplows by February. I was devastated when she died. She was eighty-nine, so it wasn't exactly a shock, but you're never really ready to lose your mother, are you? And I was sad for months and months. Every time I saw a blue jay—that was her absolute favorite bird, she had feeders set up all across her backyard—I would just tear up right there on the spot. 

But even then, feeling that low, I never stopped functioning. Not for a week, not for a month. We had to sort through her entire house, sixty years of accumulated memories. I was the one who organized the estate sale. I sat there in her dining room and individually priced her antique teacups—she had a magnificent collection of Royal Albert bone china, the Old Country Roses pattern, just beautiful with those delicate little gold rims. You have to hand-wash those, you know, you can never put them in the dishwasher or the gold flakes right off. I priced every single one of them, I managed the sale, I went back to my shifts at the store, I paid my bills. I was grieving, yes, but my life kept running right on schedule. 

So, no. I have never experienced a time where I couldn't function for weeks or months. Never. This... whatever this is right now... it is the very first time my engine has just completely stalled out.

Well, yes, doctor, I... I suppose I have. I mentioned the television programs, but it's really everything. It's just everything. I used to be such a busy woman, you know. I was always doing something.

We used to sing "How Great Thou Art" and I'd feel this wonderful lift in my spirit, just so happy to be there singing praises. And the knitting circle on Tuesday afternoons... oh, we used to have such a lovely time. I made a beautiful yellow afghan for my grandson when he was born, with the little cable knit pattern that took me three weeks to get right. We'd sit and drink Earl Grey tea and talk about the neighborhood. And Thursday nights was bingo at the community center. I wasn't a big gambler, mind you, just a few cards, but I loved the social part of it, seeing everyone, having a laugh when the caller would make a joke. 

And on nice days, especially in the spring when the dogwoods were blooming, I used to love walking through Patterson Park. I'd put on my good walking shoes—the white ones with the arch support because of my knees—and I'd walk all the way around the duck pond. I used to bring a little bag of oats for the ducks, because bread isn't good for them, you know. 

But now... now I don't do any of it. None of it. I just sit in my chair by the window. The knitting needles are still in the basket next to the sofa, right where I left them months ago. Betty called twice to see if I was coming back to choir, but I couldn't even bring myself to call her back. I just... none of it feels worth getting dressed for anymore. Putting on clothes, brushing my hair, putting on a bit of lipstick... it all just feels so pointless when my soul is so heavy. Why would I go sing hymns or play bingo when I'm carrying this terrible burden? It wouldn't be right. And honestly, I just don't have the energy or the desire to even try. It's all just gone.

I was always the one organizing the neighborhood potlucks, making sure everyone brought something different so we didn't end up with three potato salads. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a manic or hypomanic episode, which would help differentiate between major depressive disorder (F32.3), recurrent depressive disorder (F33.3), and persistent mild depressive disorder (F34.1)
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a time when you felt unusually excited, overly confident, or needed less sleep than usual for several days or more?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania or hypomania (feeling unusually excited, overly confident, or needing less sleep), which are not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens no. No, I've never been that sort of person. Unusually excited or overly confident? That just isn't me, doctor. I've always been very level-headed, very down-to-earth. My mother used to say I was born middle-aged because I never had that wild, flighty phase most girls go through. Even back in high school, while the other girls were swooning over singers or staying up all night at slumber parties, I was just... well, sensible. 

And as for sleep... goodness, I have always, always needed my rest. You simply can't work on your feet for forty years at a cash register if you don't get your proper sleep. Your back gives out, your arches ache... no, I would go to bed at 10:00 PM on the dot, every single night. I had one of those digital alarm clocks with the red numbers—the kind that are so bright they almost keep you awake if you face them toward the bed, so I always had to turn mine slightly toward the little oak nightstand. And I would wake up at 6:00 AM. Eight solid hours. 

Even when something truly wonderful happened, like when my husband surprised me with a trip to Branson, Missouri for our 25th anniversary—which was just lovely, by the way, we saw some wonderful shows, though the seats in the theater were terribly stiff on the lower back—I still went to bed at my usual time. I didn't stay up all night buzzing with excitement or feeling like I could conquer the world. I just don't have that kind of... wild energy, I suppose. I've always been steady as a rock. Never too high up in the clouds. I just kept my feet on the ground and got my eight hours.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had any previous episodes of major depression that might support a diagnosis of Recurrent Major Depressive Disorder (F33.3) or if this is a new, first episode, which would support Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode (F32.3).
doctor.question: Has anything like this ever happened to you before—where you felt so low and unable to function—that lasted for weeks or months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of past depressive episodes, which is not covered in the current symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I feel like we are sort of dancing to the exact same tune here, aren't we? I know you have to be absolutely sure, and I don't fault you for it. It’s a bit like when I used to train the new girls at the registers—I always told them, "You have to check the bottom of the grocery cart twice, every single time, because people will leave a heavy twenty-four pack of soda or a giant bag of dog food down there and just walk right out the door without paying." You have to check twice to be thorough. I understand that. 

But I promise you, checking the bottom of my cart again isn't going to turn up anything new. No. Never for weeks, never for months. 

I mean, of course I’ve had periods of mourning that lasted a long time. When my mother passed away... oh, goodness, that was back in 1998. It was a terrible, bitter winter that year, ice on all the roads, and the city actually ran out of salt for the snowplows by February. I was devastated when she died. She was eighty-nine, so it wasn't exactly a shock, but you're never really ready to lose your mother, are you? And I was sad for months and months. Every time I saw a blue jay—that was her absolute favorite bird, she had feeders set up all across her backyard—I would just tear up right there on the spot. 

But even then, feeling that low, I never stopped functioning. Not for a week, not for a month. We had to sort through her entire house, sixty years of accumulated memories. I was the one who organized the estate sale. I sat there in her dining room and individually priced her antique teacups—she had a magnificent collection of Royal Albert bone china, the Old Country Roses pattern, just beautiful with those delicate little gold rims. You have to hand-wash those, you know, you can never put them in the dishwasher or the gold flakes right off. I priced every single one of them, I managed the sale, I went back to my shifts at the store, I paid my bills. I was grieving, yes, but my life kept running right on schedule. 

So, no. I have never experienced a time where I couldn't function for weeks or months. Never. This... whatever this is right now... it is the very first time my engine has just completely stalled out.

There is no history of prior depressive episodes or manic/hypomanic episodes, ruling out recurrent depression (F33.3) and persistent mood disorders like dysthymia (F34.1).
